The buggy method is:

`org.joda.time.chrono.ZonedChronology.ZonedDateTimeField.set(long, int)`

Diagnosis:
- All failing APIs (`withHourOfDay`, `withMinuteOfHour`, `withSecondOfMinute`, `withMillisOfSecond`) delegate to a chronology field `set(...)`.
- In `DateTime`, these methods are simple wrappers:
  - `withHourOfDay(int)` → `getChronology().hourOfDay().set(getMillis(), hour)`
  - `withMinuteOfHour(int)` → `...minuteOfHour().set(...)`
  - `withSecondOfMinute(int)` → `...secondOfMinute().set(...)`
  - `withMillisOfSecond(int)` → `...millisOfSecond().set(...)`
- In a zoned chronology, that reaches `ZonedChronology.ZonedDateTimeField.set(long, int)`:

```java
public long set(long instant, int value) {
    long localInstant = iZone.convertUTCToLocal(instant);
    localInstant = iField.set(localInstant, value);
    long result = iZone.convertLocalToUTC(localInstant, false);
    if (get(result) != value) {
        throw new IllegalFieldValueException(...);
    }
    return result;
}
```

Root cause:
- This method converts the original UTC instant to local time, changes one field, then converts the ambiguous local time back to UTC using:
  - `iZone.convertLocalToUTC(localInstant, false)`
- During a DST overlap, the local wall time is ambiguous. That conversion does not preserve the original offset branch; it re-resolves the local time and may choose the other valid offset.
- That exactly matches the failures:
  - Paris overlap switches from `+02:00` to `+01:00`
  - New York overlap switches from `-05:00` to `-04:00`
  - US/Central and Australia/NSW similarly pick the wrong side of the overlap
  - Even setting a field to the same visible value can flip offset, which should not happen

Why this method, not `DateTimeZone.convertLocalToUTC`:
- `convertLocalToUTC(..., false)` is behaving according to its own overlap-resolution rules.
- The bug is that `ZonedDateTimeField.set` uses it in a context where the original offset should be retained when possible.
- The failing behavior is specifically in field-setting on an existing instant in an overlap, so the preservation policy belongs here.

Dynamic verification:
- The runtime verification attempt was inconclusive due debugger attachment failure, not due to contradictory evidence.
- Static evidence is strong and consistent across all failures.

- All failing APIs (`withHourOfDay`, `withMinuteOfHour`, `withSecondOfMinute`, `withMillisOfSecond`) delegate to a chronology field `set(...)`.
- In `DateTime`, these methods are simple wrappers:
  - `withHourOfDay(int)` → `getChronology().hourOfDay().set(getMillis(), hour)`
  - `withMinuteOfHour(int)` → `...minuteOfHour().set(...)`
  - `withSecondOfMinute(int)` → `...secondOfMinute().set(...)`

- In a zoned chronology, that reaches `ZonedChronology.ZonedDateTimeField.set(long, int)`:

```java
public long set(long instant, int value) {
    long localInstant = iZone.convertUTCToLocal(instant);
    localInstant = iField.set(localInstant, value);

Root cause:
- This method converts the original UTC instant to local time, changes one field, then converts the ambiguous local time back to UTC using:
  - `iZone.convertLocalToUTC(localInstant, false)`
- During a DST overlap, the local wall time is ambiguous. That conversion does not preserve the original offset branch; it re-resolves the local time and may choose the other valid offset.
- That exactly matches the failures:
  - Paris overlap switches from `+02:00` to `+01:00`
  - New York overlap switches from `-05:00` to `-04:00`
  - US/Central and Australia/NSW similarly pick the wrong side of the overlap
  - Even setting a field to the same visible value can flip offset, which should not happen

Why this method, not `DateTimeZone.convertLocalToUTC`:
- `convertLocalToUTC(..., false)` is behaving according to its own overlap-resolution rules.
- The bug is that `ZonedDateTimeField.set` uses it in a context where the original offset should be retained when possible.
- The failing behavior is specifically in field-setting on an existing instant in an overlap, so the preservation policy belongs here.
